q: What algorithm do bingo card generators use?
a: A well-built generator uses a Fisher-Yates shuffle: it walks the number pool once, swapping each position with a randomly chosen earlier one. It's fast and produces a provably even, unbiased order where every possible layout is equally likely.

q: Is a random bingo generator truly random?
a: It uses a pseudo-random number generator (a PRNG) — statistically random, but determined by a starting value. For a game that's ideal: you don't need casino-grade randomness, you need an even distribution with no repeats, which a good PRNG plus a Fisher-Yates shuffle delivers.

q: Why is sorting by RAND() a bad way to shuffle?
a: Sorting a column by a random key can be subtly biased, so some orderings come up more often than others; spreadsheets also re-randomize on every recalculation, and a sort has no memory of the other cards, so nothing prevents duplicates. Fisher-Yates avoids all three.

q: Can I generate the exact same bingo cards again?
a: Only with a seeded generator — the seed is the starting value that makes a batch reproducible. Most casual generators don't expose a seed, and that's fine; reproducibility is a feature of how the randomness is started, not a flaw in it.
